cur:objects-berlin-diptych-christ-and-vi.summary: On the left leaf a bearded Christ sits enthroned beneath a shell-headed niche, holding a jewelled book and blessing, flanked by Saints Peter and Paul; on the right leaf the Virgin sits enthroned with the Christ Child on her lap, between two archangels. The two leaves answer each other as the heavenly King and his Mother, each attended by a celestial court. This imperial-looking pair is among the most majestic Christian ivories of the age of Justinian.
facts: Pairing Christ enthroned among apostles with the Virgin enthroned among angels on facing leaves became a model for later Byzantine icon pairs on templon screens (type).
The leaves follow the format of the official consular diptychs of the period, but replace the consul with Christ and the Virgin (type).
cur:objects-berlin-diptych-christ-and-vi.notes: Museum record not accessible; the attribution to Constantinople is the usual one in the literature.

wga:zearly/1/4mosaics/2ravenna/1galla/2l.summary: In a rocky green landscape beneath a starry blue vault, the young Christ sits among six sheep, reaching across to touch one that turns toward him. He wears a golden tunic with a purple mantle and a golden halo, and holds a tall golden cross instead of a shepherd's crook. The image fuses the gentle shepherd of the Gospel with the majesty of a ruler, one of the most beloved mosaics of the 5th century.
facts: The lunette is set over the north entrance of the building, built between 425 and 450 as a chapel adjoining the church of Santa Croce in Ravenna.
Despite its name, the empress Galla Placidia was not buried here; she died in Rome in 450, and the tradition of her burial in Ravenna dates from the 13th century.
The figure of a shepherd carrying a sheep was adopted from ancient art into Christian funerary art from the late 3rd century; here the shepherd is in imperial purple and gold.
